newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss envoy targets U.S., U.K. on Holocaust funds.
newsitem.headline: Swiss envoy targets U.S., U.K. on Holocaust funds.

text.p: Switzerland's diplomatic troubleshooter said his ambassadors told him on Friday Berne would have to work hardest in the United States and Britain to counter allegations that the Swiss profited from the Holocaust.

Diplomat Thomas Borer said a meeting of Swiss envoys from 12 countries including the U.S., Britain, Israel and major European capitals helped his ongoing task of formulating a strategy for better presenting Switzerland's defence.
"We realised that the issue is more pressing in some countries than in others, most of all in the United States but also in Britain," Borer told Reuters after the meeting.

Borer is in charge of a diplomatic task force created to toughen Berne's often meek responses to a wave of criticism headed by the New York-based World Jewish Congress (WJC), U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato and British member of parliament Greville Janner, a WJC vice-president.
The task force was set up by Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti in late October as the government went on the offensive after weeks of leaving the issue to lower-ranking officials.

Borer's talks with the ambassadors was part of a hectic series of meetings as he forges a strategy for convincing critics that Switzerland is serious about probing its financial role before and during World War Two.
"We talked about how Switzerland could best communicate its message," he said about the session with ambassadors.
Berne politicians and Swiss banks have voiced frustration that foreign critics are sceptical of three separate inquiries started this year or now being set up.
Swiss banks charged an ombudsman at the start of the year with aiding searches by the heirs of Holocaust victims for swiss bank acounts they believe were being hidden by the banks.

To probe charges of a Swiss cover-up, major Jewish groups and Swiss banks then agreed in May to set up an independent panel headed by former U.S. Federal Reserve Board chairman Paul Volcker to search for any wealth that escaped two previous sweeps by banks.
The commission will also work with a historical panel due to win parliament's approval next month with a broad mandate to probe Switzerland's wartime role as a financial centre.

Both the Volcker commission and the government panel will be empowered to lift banking secrecy to probe dormant wartime-era accounts, although these powers will not compromise the confidentiality of accounts held by modern customers.

Meanwhile, Switzerland's association of lawyers said it would investigate a list of attorneys named by U.S. secret service agents in the 1940s in connection with allegations of helping hide Nazi loot or assets left by Holocaust victims.

Association president Ulrich Hirt told Reuters he would try to find more information about the 86 names sent to him by D'Amato, whose Senate Banking Committee is probing the Swiss financial role in World War Two.

Hirt said only two of the names still turned up in current membership rolls and noted that the same list had appeared in Swiss newspapers in 1990, although D'Amato said the document was secret until being declassified by the U.S. government recently.
Hirt said the association had already written to members in August to ask whether they still administered any accounts for Jews killed inthe Holocaust or knew of any such lost assets.
Replies so far had turned up no hidden wealth, he said.
